title: Hybrid client-side reservation + probabilistic server dedupe for at-least-once ingest
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: We observe duplicate charge events and quota miscounts in edge scenarios where clients retry requests (network timeouts or 5xx), combined with aggressive client-side backoff and gateway-level retries. Existing per-request ingest token approaches either force synchronous global coordination (high latency) or rely on large in-memory ledgers (costly).

Goal: Produce a pragmatic, rollout-friendly system that prevents duplicate billing/consumption while preserving at-least-once semantics for application-level delivery and keeping tail latency low. The solution must operate across hosted and Dedicated/Private deployments, integrate with rate limiting/quota accounting, and provide clear observability for reconciliation and customer support.

Proposed approach (hybrid):
1) Client-side ephemeral reservation token (CRT):
   - On initial client send, SDK generates a compact reservation token: versioned nonce + issuing customer id hash + short TTL (e.g., 60s) + HMAC signature with per-customer key (for Private/Dedicated we use customer KMS).
   - CRT is returned by the front-door (edge) when it accepts a request and is echoed by the client on retries. CRT indicates: "I already reserved capacity for this logical request."

2) Two-phase consumption accounting at the server:
   - Soft-reserve stage: Front-door increments a lightweight in-memory reservation counter and attaches CRT to the inflight request metadata. This is cheap, bounded by TTL, and used to block double-charge at the edge path.
   - Finalize stage: When the request completes without retry-caused duplication, the backend emits a commit entry into the per-customer finalization ledger (append-only, storage-backed). Only commit entries are used for billing.

3) Probabilistic server-side duplicate detection:
   - To protect against lost or malformed CRTs (old clients) and eventual consistency edge cases, we maintain a per-customer sliding Bloom filter + reservoir-sampled audit index that records recent commit fingerprints (small footprint).
   - Bloom filter parameters tuned for customer profile (expected QPS) to bound false positives under a target FPR (e.g., <=0.05%). When a commit arrives that appears in the Bloom filter, it is treated as a probable duplicate and reconciled via the audit index rather than immediately charged.

4) Billing semantics and quotas:
   - Reservations decrement an "available-reserve" view that affects immediate rate-limiter decisions (prevents simultaneous bursts from the same logical request). However, only final ledger commits decrement the customer's actual quota/billing counters.
   - If a reservation expires and no commit arrives, reservation is recycled; no charge occurs. If a commit arrives with no prior reservation (older client), commit is accepted and charged after duplicate detection checks.

5) Reconciliation & Escalation:
   - Periodic background reconciliation jobs sample the reservoir audit index and reconcile blurred cases where Bloom filter says duplicate but ledger lacks definitive evidence. Reconciliation has two modes: auto-debit (rare, when commit fingerprint exists in durable store) and manual investigation flagging.
   - For high-value customers, enable stronger guarantees (optional feature) by switching to deterministic commit ledgers with explicit client nonce coordination — traded off for higher latencies and storage costs.

Design decisions and trade-offs:
- Why hybrid? Full determinism (global dedupe table) is expensive at scale and costly for Dedicated/Private. Pure probabilistic dedupe risks false positives that could underbill (customer wrongfully not charged) or overbill if we double-charge. The hybrid minimizes both risks by using reservation tokens for common-case dedupe and probabilistic structures plus reconciliation for edge cases.
- Bloom filter false positives vs billing correctness: we prefer false positives that produce extra reconciliation work (customer support) over false negatives that cause double-billing. Bloom filter parameters therefore bias to slightly higher FPR but aggressive reconciliation policy.
- Client complexity: CRT requires minimal SDK work (one HMAC + attach token). Backward compatibility: server accepts requests without CRT but routes them through stronger duplicate detection.

Telemetry & Observability:
- Metrics to surface: reservation_accept_rate, reservation_collision_rate, commit_without_reservation_rate, bloom_positive_rate, reconciliation_count, reconciled_charge_corrections, customer-impacting-false-positive-rate.
- Dashboards: per-customer heatmap of reservation vs commit divergence, SLA alerts when commit_without_reservation_rate > 0.1% for top 100 customers.
- Audit logs: all commit fingerprints are retained for 90 days in the audit index (configurable per customer for compliance).

Testing and rollout plan:
1) Unit & integration tests for CRT validation, TTL behavior, and commit path.
2) Chaos tests: simulate dropped CRTs, duplicated commits, delayed commits, and network partitions.
3) Canary rollout on staging -> small set of non-critical customers (opt-in) -> ramp 10% -> 50% -> worldwide.
4) SLOs to monitor: duplicate-billing-rate < 1 in 1e6 requests, reservation-impact-latency < 3ms p95 at edge.

Open questions and future enhancements:
- Should reservations be charged a micro-fee to mitigate spammy reservations? (Discussed with PM; leaning no.)
- How to expose CRT in 3rd-party SDKs (language portability and secure key distribution).
- For Private deployments, KMS integration model for per-customer HMAC keys needs product/legal review.

Rollout artefacts: design doc (Confluence), compatibility matrix, SDK changes, migration playbook for older clients.
